name: Calendly
headline: Easy: self-serve with no documented review. Watch for single-use refresh tokens and webhooks that need a paid Calendly plan.

firstTest.text: Sign up with GitHub or Google, create a Sandbox OAuth app and run the flow on localhost. Calendly documents no approval step.

production.text: Create a separate Production app with an HTTPS redirect address and its own client ID and secret. Calendly documents no review before other users connect.

approvalWait.text: None documented. The OAuth app pages describe no review, listing or approval step.

whoCanRegister.text: Anyone with a developer account (GitHub or Google login), separate from a Calendly user account. Webhooks and Scheduling API endpoints need a paid plan.

testMode.text: Sandbox allows localhost redirects; Production needs HTTPS. Access lasts 2 hours. Per user: 50 requests a minute (500 paid), 8 token requests a minute.

steps.title: Create a developer account
steps.detail: Sign up at developer.calendly.com with GitHub or Google. It isn't tied to any Calendly user account.

steps.title: Create the Sandbox app
steps.detail: Name it, choose web or native, set the environment to Sandbox and tick the scopes you need. Enter a redirect address; http://localhost is allowed in Sandbox.

steps.title: Copy the client secrets
steps.detail: Copy the Client ID, Client Secret and webhook signing key right after creation. You can't view the secret or signing key again, so store them in your hosting settings now.

steps.title: Build the sign-in flow
steps.detail: Send users to Calendly's sign-in page with your client ID, redirect address and the extra security check most libraries do for you. Then swap the one-time code for tokens.

steps.title: Handle single-use refresh tokens
steps.detail: Each refresh token works once and returns a new pair, so overwrite the stored one every time. If a refresh is rejected, clear the tokens and ask the user to reconnect. Access lasts 2 hours.

steps.title: Test in Sandbox
steps.detail: Connect a test Calendly account and read events. Refresh twice in a row to confirm the first refresh token is rejected when reused.

steps.title: Create the Production app
steps.detail: Create a new app with environment Production and an HTTPS redirect address, as Calendly recommends before you use customer data. Copy its new client ID, secret and signing key into your production settings.

steps.title: Add webhooks if needed
steps.detail: Subscribe through the API to booking, cancellation or routing form events. Your app needs the matching read permissions, and the user needs a paid plan.

steps.title: Respect rate limits
steps.detail: Watch the rate limit headers. After a 'too many requests' error, wait for the reset (usually 60 seconds) and back off. Creating invitees has a stricter limit, and trial accounts get 5 a day.

blockers.title: Users are disconnected after one refresh
blockers.fix: Refresh tokens work once. If two requests refresh at the same time, or you keep an older token, the second one fails. Refresh one request at a time per user, save the new token before using the new access token, and ask the user to reconnect on failure.

blockers.title: Webhooks fail or never fire
blockers.fix: You need a paid Calendly plan, the right read permissions on your app, and an owner or admin for organization-level subscriptions. Routing form submissions work only at organization level.

blockers.title: Production rejects your redirect address
blockers.fix: Production redirect addresses must be HTTPS; only Sandbox allows http://localhost. Match the address exactly to what you registered.

blockers.title: Free-plan users hit limits fast
blockers.fix: Free accounts get 50 requests per user per minute, against 500 on paid plans. Cache event lists, and queue agent calls instead of looping.

blockers.title: You lost the client secret
blockers.fix: The secret and signing key show only once and can't be viewed when you edit the app. Create a new app and update your settings.

blockers.title: Booking-link features fail for a customer
blockers.fix: Webhooks and Scheduling API endpoints need a paid plan on the user's account. Check the plan before offering them, and tell users what's missing.

agentCan: Write the sign-in flow with the extra security check, token swap and a per-user locked refresh
Store the Client ID, secret and signing key, keeping Sandbox and Production apart
Subscribe to webhooks, check their signatures and handle cancellations and reschedules
Back off on 'too many requests' errors using the rate limit headers
Spot a rejected refresh and show a reconnect prompt

Create the Sandbox and Production apps and copy the secrets the one time they are shown

drafts.title: Consent explainer before the Calendly screen
drafts.body: [Product name] will ask Calendly for permission to see your scheduled events and who booked them, and to create booking links or cancel events when you ask. We never change your availability without you approving it. You can disconnect any time from Settings in [Product name].

drafts.title: Reconnect prompt after a failed refresh
drafts.body: Your Calendly connection has stopped working. This can happen when access is revoked or expires. Choose Reconnect and sign in to Calendly again to continue.

drafts.title: Note to customers about Calendly plans
drafts.body: Live booking updates (webhooks) and booking-link creation need a paid Calendly plan. If your account is on the free plan, [Product name] will still show your events, but updates arrive when we check, not instantly.

unconfirmed: Whether Calendly reviews Production apps. No page I opened mentions a review, listing or approval, and the absence of one in the docs is not proof that none exists.
Whether Sandbox apps can connect to real Calendly accounts or only to test data, and whether Sandbox uses a different authorization host. The authorization page gives only auth.calendly.com.
Whether a connecting user's plan or the developer's plan decides webhook access. The help center says webhooks and Scheduling API endpoints need a paid plan but does not say whose.
How long a refresh token lives if it is never used. One API page says refresh tokens do not expire until they are used. The rotation guide gives no lifetime.
Whether the August 31, 2026 rotation deadline has already made single-use refresh tokens mandatory for all older apps. The guide says the grace period will end and gives no further date.
Any cap on the number of users who can connect one Production app. No page I opened states one.
